Later implants such as CHOPSTICK use a blend of HTTP and other legitimate channels, depending on …
Uses T1074 Data Staged: APT28 has stored captured credential information in a file named pi.log.
Uses T1075 Pass the Hash: APT28 has used pass the hash for lateral movement.

title: ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28
text:
ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT28 has used legitimate credentials to gain initial access, maintain access, and exfiltrate data from a victim network. The group has specifically used credentials stolen through a spearphishing email to login to the DCCC network. The group has also leveraged …
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT28 has used Forfiles to locate PDF, Excel, and Word documents during. The group also searched a compromised DCCC computer for specific terms.
Uses T1085 Rundll32: APT28 executed CHOPSTICK by using rundll32 commands such as rundll32.exe “C:\Windows\twain_64.dll”. APT28 also executed a.dll for a first stage dropper using rundll32.exe. An APT28 loader Trojan saved a batch script that uses rundll32 to execute a DLL payload.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: APT28 downloads and executes PowerShell scripts.
Uses T1090 Connection Proxy: APT28 used other victims as proxies to relay command traffic, for instance using a compromised Georgian military email server as a hop point to NATO victims. The group has also used a tool that acts as a proxy to allow …
Uses T1091 Replication Through Removable Media: APT28 uses a tool to infect connected USB devices and transmit itself to air-gapped computers when the infected USB device is inserted.
Uses T1092 Communication Through Removable Media: APT28 uses a tool that captures information from air-gapped computers via an infected USB and transfers it to network-connected computer when the USB is inserted.
Uses T1099 Timestomp: APT28 has performed timestomping on victim files.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: APT28 has downloaded additional files, including by using a first-stage downloader to contact the C2 server to obtain the second-stage implant.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: APT28 has intentionally deleted computer files to cover their tracks, including with use of the program CCleaner.

title: ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28
text:
ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: APT28 has used tools to take screenshots from victims.
Uses T1114 Email Collection: APT28 has collected emails from victim Microsoft Exchange servers.
Uses T1119 Automated Collection: APT28 used a publicly available tool to gather and compress multiple documents on the DCCC and DNC networks.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: APT28 uses a module to receive a notification every time a USB mass storage device is inserted into a victim.
Uses T1122 Component Object Model Hijacking: APT28 has used COM hijacking for persistence by replacing the legitimate MMDeviceEnumerator object with a payload.
Uses T1134 Access Token Manipulation: APT28 has used CVE-2015-1701 to access the SYSTEM token and copy it into the current process as part of privilege escalation.
Uses T1137 Office Application Startup: APT28 has used the Office Test persistence mechanism within Microsoft Office by adding the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf to execute code.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: An APT28 macro uses the command certutil -decode to decode contents of a.txt file storing the base64 encoded payload.
Uses T1143 Hidden Window: APT28 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1158 Hidden Files and Directories: APT28 has saved files with hidden file attributes.
Uses T1173 Dynamic Data Exchange: APT28 has delivered JHUHUGIT and Koadic by executing PowerShell commands through DDE in Word documents.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: APT28 sent spearphishing emails which used a URL-shortener service to masquerade as a legitimate service and to redirect targets to credential harvesting sites.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: APT28 sent spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Office attachments.
Uses T1199 Trusted Relationship: Once APT28 gained access to the DCCC network, the group then proceeded to use that access to compromise the DNC network.

title: ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28
text:
ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT28 has exploited Microsoft Office vulnerability CVE-2017-0262 for execution.
Uses T1204 User Execution: APT28 attempted to get users to click on Microsoft Office attachments containing malicious macro scripts.
Uses T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services: APT28 exploited a Windows SMB Remote Code Execution Vulnerability to conduct lateral movement.
Uses T1211 Exploitation for Defense Evasion: APT28 has used CVE-2015-4902 to bypass security features.
Uses T1213 Data from Information Repositories: APT28 has collected information from Microsoft SharePoint services within target networks.
Uses T1221 Template Injection: APT28 used weaponized Microsoft Word documents abusing the remote template function to retrieve a malicious macro.
Uses T1527 Application Access Token: APT28 has used several malicious applications that abused OAuth access tokens to gain access to target email accounts, including Gmail and Yahoo Mail.
Uses T1528 Steal Application Access Token: APT28 has used several malicious applications to steal user OAuth access tokens including applications masquerading as "Google Defender" "Google Email Protection," and "Google Scanner" for Gmail users. They also targeted Yahoo users with applications masquerading as "Delivery Service" and "McAfee …

title: ATT&CK Group G0016: APT29
text:
ATT&CK Group G0016: APT29
Associated names: YTTRIUM, The Dukes, Cozy Bear, CozyDuke.
APT29 is threat group that has been attributed to the Russian government and has operated since at least 2008. This group reportedly compromised the Democratic National Committee starting in the summer of 2015.
Uses T1015 Accessibility Features: APT29 used sticky-keys to obtain unauthenticated, privileged console access.
Uses T1023 Shortcut Modification: APT29 drops a Windows shortcut file for execution.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT29 uses PowerShell to use Base64 for obfuscation.
Uses T1043 Commonly Used Port: APT29 has used Port Number 443 for C2.
Uses T1045 Software Packing: APT29 used UPX to pack files.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: APT29 used WMI to steal credentials and execute backdoors at a future time.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: APT29 used named and hijacked scheduled tasks to establish persistence.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT29 added Registry Run keys to establish persistence.
Uses T1064 Scripting: APT29 has used encoded PowerShell scripts uploaded to CozyCar installations to download and install SeaDuke, as well as to evade defenses.
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal on Host: APT29 used SDelete to remove artifacts from victims.
Uses T1084 Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription: APT29 has used WMI event filters to establish persistence.
Uses T1085 Rundll32: APT29 has used rundll32.exe for execution.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: APT29 has used encoded PowerShell scripts uploaded to CozyCar installations to download and install SeaDuke. APT29 also used PowerShell scripts to evade defenses.
Uses T1088 Bypass User Account Control: APT29 has bypassed UAC.
Uses T1095 Standard Non-Application Layer Protocol: APT29 uses TCP for C2 communications.
Uses T1097 Pass the Ticket: APT29 used Kerberos ticket attacks for lateral movement.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: APT29 used SDelete to remove artifacts from victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0016: APT29
text:
ATT&CK Group G0016: APT29
Uses T1172 Domain Fronting: APT29 has used the meek domain fronting plugin for Tor to hide the destination of C2 traffic.
Uses T1188 Multi-hop Proxy: A backdoor used by APT29 created a Tor hidden service to forward traffic from the Tor client to local ports 3389 (RDP), 139 (Netbios), and 445 (SMB) enabling full remote access from outside the network.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: APT29 has used spearphishing with a link to trick victims into clicking on a link to a zip file containing malicious files.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: APT29 has used spearphishing emails with an attachment to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT29 has used multiple software exploits for common client software, like Microsoft Word and Adobe Reader, to gain code execution as part of.
Uses T1204 User Execution: APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to open links or attachments, including, but not limited to, malicious Microsoft Word documents,.pdf, and.lnk files.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Associated names: Gothic Panda, Pirpi, UPS Team, Buckeye, Threat Group-0110, TG-0110.
APT3 is a China-based threat group that researchers have attributed to China's Ministry of State Security. This group is responsible for the campaigns known as Operation Clandestine Fox, Operation Clandestine Wolf, and Operation Double Tap. As of June 2015, the group appears to have shifted from targeting primarily US victims to primarily political organizations in Hong Kong. 

MITRE has also developed an APT3 Adversary Emulation Plan.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: APT3 has used tools to compress data before exfilling it.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: APT3 has used a tool to dump credentials by injecting itself into lsass.exe and triggering with the argument "dig." The group has also used a tools to dump passwords from browsers.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT3 will identify Microsoft Office documents on the victim's computer.
Uses T1015 Accessibility Features: APT3 replaces the Sticky Keys binary C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe for persistence.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: A keylogging tool used by APT3 gathers network information from the victim, including the MAC address, IP address, WINS, DHCP server, and gateway.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can detect the existence of remote systems.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT3 obfuscates files or information to help evade defensive measures.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: An APT3 downloader uses the Windows command "cmd.exe" /C whoami to verify that it is running with the elevated privileges of “System.”
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over Command and Control Channel: APT3 has a tool that exfiltrates data over the C2 channel.
Uses T1043 Commonly Used Port: APT3 uses commonly used ports (like HTTPS/443) for command and control.
Uses T1045 Software Packing: APT3 has been known to pack their tools.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can enumerate current network connections.
Uses T1050 New Service: APT3 has a tool that creates a new service for persistence.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: An APT3 downloader creates persistence by creating the following scheduled task: schtasks /create /tn "mysc" /tr C:\Users\Public\test.exe /sc ONLOGON /ru "System".
Uses T1056 Input Capture: APT3 has used a keylogging tool that records keystrokes in encrypted files.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can list out currently running processes.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: An APT3 downloader uses the Windows command "cmd.exe" /C whoami. The group also uses a tool to execute commands on remote computers.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT3 places scripts in the startup folder for persistence.
Uses T1061 Graphical User Interface: APT3 has interacted with compromised systems to browse and copy files through its graphical user interface in Remote Desktop Protocol sessions.
Uses T1064 Scripting: APT3 has used PowerShell on victim systems to download and run payloads after exploitation.
Uses T1065 Uncommonly Used Port: An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections to two separate IP addresses over TCP port 1913 and TCP port 81.
Uses T1066 Indicator Removal from Tools: APT3 has been known to remove indicators of compromise from tools.
Uses T1069 Permission Groups Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can enumerate the permissions associated with Windows groups.
Uses T1073 DLL Side-Loading: APT3 has been known to side load DLLs with a valid version of Chrome with one of their tools.
Uses T1074 Data Staged: APT3 has been known to stage files for exfiltration in a single location.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT3 enables the Remote Desktop Protocol for persistence.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Uses T1077 Windows Admin Shares: APT3 will copy files over to Windows Admin Shares (like ADMIN$) as part of lateral movement.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT3 leverages valid accounts after gaining credentials for use within the victim domain.
Uses T1081 Credentials in Files: APT3 has a tool that can locate credentials in files on the file system such as those from Firefox or Chrome.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can obtain information about the local system.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT3 has a tool that looks for files and directories on the local file system.
Uses T1085 Rundll32: APT3 has a tool that can run DLLs.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: APT3 has used PowerShell on victim systems to download and run payloads after exploitation.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: APT3 has used a tool that can obtain info about local and global group users, power users, and administrators.
Uses T1090 Connection Proxy: An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections for its initial C2.
Uses T1095 Standard Non-Application Layer Protocol: An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections for its initial C2.
Uses T1098 Account Manipulation: APT3 has been known to add created accounts to local admin groups to maintain elevated access.
Uses T1104 Multi-Stage Channels: An APT3 downloader first establishes a SOCKS5 connection to 192.157.198[.]103 using TCP port 1913; once the server response is verified, it then requests a connection to 192.184.60[.]229 on TCP port 81.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: APT3 has a tool that can copy files to remote machines.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: APT3 has a tool that can delete files.
Uses T1108 Redundant Access: APT3 has been known to use multiple backdoors per campaign.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Uses T1110 Brute Force: APT3 has been known to brute force password hashes to be able to leverage plain text credentials.
Uses T1136 Create Account: APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, such as support_388945a0.
Uses T1143 Hidden Window: APT3 has been known to use -WindowStyle Hidden to conceal PowerShell windows.

title: ATT&CK Group G0013: APT30
text:
ATT&CK Group G0013: APT30
APT30 is a threat group suspected to be associated with the Chinese government. While Naikon shares some characteristics with APT30, the two groups do not appear to be exact matches.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Associated names: SeaLotus, OceanLotus, APT-C-00.
APT32 is a threat group that has been active since at least 2014. The group has targeted multiple private sector industries as well as with foreign governments, dissidents, and journalists with a strong focus on Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, the Philippines, Laos, and Cambodia. They have extensively used strategic web compromises to compromise victims. The group is believed to be Vietnam-based.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: APT32's backdoor has used LZMA compression before exfiltration.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: APT32 used Mimikatz, GetPassword_x64, and customized versions of Windows Credential Dumper, HookChangePassword, and Outlook Credential Dumper to harvest credentials.
Uses T1009 Binary Padding: APT32 includes garbage code to mislead anti-malware software and researchers.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: APT32's backdoor can query the Windows Registry to gather system information.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: APT32 used the ipconfig /all command to gather the IP address from the system.
Uses T1017 Application Deployment Software: APT32 compromised McAfee ePO to move laterally by distributing malware as a software deployment task.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: APT32 used the net view command to show all shares available, including the administrative shares such as C$ and ADMIN$. APT32 also used the ping command.
Uses T1022 Data Encrypted: APT32 backdoors have encrypted data before exfiltration, including by using RC4 encryption.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT32 uses the Invoke-Obfuscation framework to obfuscate their PowerShell and also performs other code obfuscation. APT32 has also encoded payloads using Base64 and a framework called "Dont-Kill-My-Cat (DKMC). APT32 also encrypts the library used for network exfiltration with AES-256 in …
Uses T1031 Modify Existing Service: APT32 modified Windows Services to ensure PowerShell scripts were loaded on the system.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT32 collected the victim's username and executed the whoami command on the victim's machine.
Uses T1035 Service Execution: APT32's backdoor has used Windows services as a way to execute its malicious payload.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: APT32 has used hidden or non-printing characters to help masquerade file names on a system, such as appending a Unicode no-break space character to a legitimate service name. They have also used by moving and renaming pubprn.vbs to a.txt file …
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over Command and Control Channel: APT32's backdoor has exfiltrated data using the already opened channel with its C&C server.
Uses T1043 Commonly Used Port: APT32 has used port 80 for C2 communications.
Uses T1046 Network Service Scanning: APT32 performed network scanning on the network to search for open ports, services, OS finger-printing, and other vulnerabilities.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: APT32 used WMI to deploy their tools on remote machines and to gather information about the Outlook process.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT32 used the netstat -anpo tcp command to display TCP connections on the victim's machine.
Uses T1050 New Service: APT32 creates a Windows service to establish persistence.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: APT32 has used scheduled tasks to persist on victim systems.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: APT32 has used cmd.exe for execution.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT32 established persistence using Registry Run keys, both to execute PowerShell and VBS scripts as well as to execute their backdoor directly.
Uses T1064 Scripting: APT32 has used macros, PowerShell scripts, COM scriptlets, and VBS scripts.
Uses T1065 Uncommonly Used Port: APT32 backdoor can use HTTP over an uncommon TCP port (e.g 14146) which is specified in the backdoor configuration.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: APT32 has used CVE-2016-7255 to escalate privileges.
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal on Host: APT32 has cleared select event log entries.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: APT32 has used JavaScript that communicates over HTTP or HTTPS to attacker controlled domains to download additional frameworks. The group has also used email for C2 via an Office macro. The group's backdoor can also exfiltrate data by encoding it …
Uses T1073 DLL Side-Loading: APT32 ran legitimately-signed executables from Symantec and McAfee which load a malicious DLL. The group also side-loads its backdoor by dropping a library and a legitimate, signed executable (AcroTranscoder).
Uses T1075 Pass the Hash: APT32 has used pass the hash for lateral movement.
Uses T1077 Windows Admin Shares: APT32 used Net to use Windows' hidden network shares to copy their tools to remote machines for execution.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT32 has used legitimate local admin account credentials.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT32 has collected the OS version and computer name from victims. One of the group's backdoors can also query the Windows Registry to gather system information, and another macOS backdoor performs a fingerprint of the machine on its first connection …
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT32's backdoor possesses the capability to list files and directories on a machine.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: APT32 has used PowerShell-based tools, PowerShell one-liners, and shellcode loaders for execution.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: APT32 enumerated administrative users and DC servers using the commands net localgroup administrators and net group "Domain Controllers" /domain.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1094 Custom Command and Control Protocol: APT32 uses Cobalt Strike's malleable C2 functionality to blend in with network traffic. The group's backdoor can also exfiltrate data by encoding it in the subdomain field of DNS packets. Additionally, one of the group's macOS backdoors implements a specific …
Uses T1096 NTFS File Attributes: APT32 used NTFS alternate data stream to hide their payloads.
Uses T1097 Pass the Ticket: APT32 successfully gained remote access by using pass the ticket.
Uses T1099 Timestomp: APT32 has used scheduled task raw XML with a backdated timestamp of June 2, 2016. The group has also set the creation time of the files dropped by the second stage of the exploit to match the creation time of …
Uses T1100 Web Shell: APT32 has used Web shells to maintain access to victim websites.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: APT32 has added JavaScript to victim websites to download additional frameworks that profile and compromise website visitors.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: APT32's macOS backdoor can receive a “delete” command.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: APT32's backdoor has modified the Windows Registry to store the backdoor's configuration.
Uses T1117 Regsvr32: APT32 created a Scheduled Task that used regsvr32.exe to execute a COM scriptlet that dynamically downloaded a backdoor and injected it into memory. The group has also used regsvr32 to run their backdoor.
Uses T1137 Office Application Startup: APT32 installed a backdoor macro in Microsoft Outlook for persistence.
Uses T1143 Hidden Window: APT32 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1158 Hidden Files and Directories: APT32's macOS backdoor hides the clientID file via a chflags function.
Uses T1170 Mshta: APT32 has used mshta.exe for code execution.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: APT32 has infected victims by tricking them into visiting compromised watering hole websites.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: APT32 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious links.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: APT32 has sent spearphishing emails with a malicious executable disguised as a document or spreadsheet.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT32 has used RTF document that includes an exploit to execute malicious code. (CVE-2017-11882)
Uses T1204 User Execution: APT32 has attempted to lure users to execute a malicious dropper delivered via a spearphishing attachment.
Uses T1216 Signed Script Proxy Execution: APT32 has used PubPrn.vbs within execution scripts to execute malware, possibly bypassing defenses.
Uses T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification: APT32's macOS backdoor changes the permission of the file it wants to execute to 755.

title: ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
text:
ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
Associated names: Elfin.
APT33 is a suspected Iranian threat group that has carried out operations since at least 2013. The group has targeted organizations across multiple industries in the United States, Saudi Arabia, and South Korea, with a particular interest in the aviation and energy sectors.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: APT33 has used WinRAR to compress data prior to exfil.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne, Mimikatz, Gpppassword, SniffPass, and ProcDump to dump credentials.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT33 has used base64 to encode payloads.
Uses T1032 Standard Cryptographic Protocol: APT33 has used AES for encryption of command and control traffic.
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: APT33 has used SniffPass to collect credentials by sniffing network traffic.
Uses T1043 Commonly Used Port: APT33 has used port 443 for command and control.
Uses T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: APT33 has used FTP to exfiltrate files (separately from the C2 channel).
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: APT33 has created a scheduled task to execute a.vbe file multiple times a day.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT33 has deployed a tool known as DarkComet to the Startup folder of a victim.
Uses T1065 Uncommonly Used Port: APT33 has used ports 808 and 880 for command and control.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: APT33 has used a publicly available exploit for CVE-2017-0213 to escalate privileges on a local system.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: APT33 has used HTTP for command and control.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT33 has used valid accounts for initial access and privilege escalation.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: APT33 has utilized PowerShell to download files from the C2 server and run various scripts.

title: ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
text:
ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: APT33 has downloaded additional files and programs from its C2 server.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: APT33 has used password spraying to gain access to target systems.
Uses T1132 Data Encoding: APT33 has used base64 to encode command and control traffic.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: APT33 has sent spearphishing emails containing links to.hta files.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT33 has attempted to exploit a known vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2018-20250).
Uses T1204 User Execution: APT33 has lured users to click links to malicious HTML applications delivered via spearphishing emails.
Uses T1480 Execution Guardrails: APT33 has used kill dates in their malware to guardrail execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
text:
ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
Associated names: ScarCruft, Reaper, Group123, TEMP.Reaper.
APT37 is a suspected North Korean cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. The group has targeted victims primarily in South Korea, but also in Japan, Vietnam, Russia, Nepal, China, India, Romania, Kuwait, and other parts of the Middle East. APT37 has also been linked to following campaigns between 2016-2018: Operation Daybreak, Operation Erebus, Golden Time, Evil New Year, Are you Happy?, FreeMilk, Northern Korean Human Rights, and Evil New Year 2018. 

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and the name Lazarus Group is known to encompass a broad range of activity. Some organizations use the name Lazarus Group to refer to any activity attributed to North Korea. Some organizations track North Korean clusters or groups such as Bluenoroff, APT37, and APT38 separately, while other organizations may track some activity associated with those group names by the name Lazarus Group.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: APT37 has used a credential stealer known as ZUMKONG that can harvest usernames and passwords stored in browsers.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT37 has collected data from victims' local systems.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT37 sends images to users that are embedded with shellcode. The group also obfuscates strings and payloads, including through the use of steganography.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT37 identifies the victim username.
Uses T1043 Commonly Used Port: APT37 has used port 8080 for C2.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT37 injects its malware variant, ROKRAT, into the cmd.exe process.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT37's Freenki malware lists running processes using the Microsoft Windows API.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: APT37 has used the command-line interface.

title: ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
text:
ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT37's has added persistence via the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\CurrentVersion\Run\.
Uses T1064 Scripting: APT37 executes shellcode and a script to decode Base64 strings.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: APT37 uses HTTPS to conceal C2 communications.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT37 collects the computer name, the BIOS model, and execution path.
Uses T1088 Bypass User Account Control: APT37 has a function in the initial dropper to bypass Windows UAC in order to execute the next payload with higher privileges.
Uses T1094 Custom Command and Control Protocol: APT37 credential stealer ZUMKONG emails credentials from the victim using HTTP POST requests.
Uses T1102 Web Service: APT37 leverages social networking sites and cloud platforms (AOL, Twitter, Yandex, Mediafire, pCloud, Dropbox, and Box) for C2.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: APT37 has downloaded second stage malware from compromised websites.
Uses T1106 Execution through API: APT37 leverages the Windows API calls: VirtualAlloc(), WriteProcessMemory(), and CreateRemoteThread() for process injection.
Uses T1116 Code Signing: APT37 has signed its malware with an invalid digital certificates listed as “Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Company Limited.”
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: APT37 has a Bluetooth device harvester, which uses Windows Bluetooth APIs to find information on connected Bluetooth devices.
Uses T1123 Audio Capture: APT37 has used an audio capturing utility known as SOUNDWAVE that captures microphone input.
Uses T1173 Dynamic Data Exchange: APT37 has used Windows DDE for execution of commands and a malicious VBS.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: APT37 has used strategic web compromises, particularly of South Korean websites, to distribute malware. The group has also used torrent file-sharing sites to more indiscriminately disseminate malware to victims. As part of their compromises, the group has used a Javascript …

title: ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
text:
ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: APT37 delivers malware using spearphishing emails with malicious HWP attachments.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT37 has used Flash Player (CVE-2016-4117, CVE-2018-4878) and Word (CVE-2017-0199) exploits for execution.
Uses T1204 User Execution: APT37 has sent spearphishing attachments attempting to get a user to open them.
Uses T1487 Disk Structure Wipe: APT37 has access to destructive malware that is capable of overwriting a machine's Master Boot Record (MBR).
Uses T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: APT37 has used malware that will issue the command shutdown /r /t 1 to reboot a system after wiping its MBR.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
APT38 is a financially-motivated threat group that is backed by the North Korean regime. The group mainly targets banks and financial institutions and has targeted more than 16 organizations in at least 13 countries since at least 2014.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and the name Lazarus Group is known to encompass a broad range of activity. Some organizations use the name Lazarus Group to refer to any activity attributed to North Korea. Some organizations track North Korean clusters or groups such as Bluenoroff, APT37, and APT38 separately, while other organizations may track some activity associated with those group names by the name Lazarus Group.
Uses T1045 Software Packing: APT38 has used several code packing methods such as Themida, Enigma, VMProtect, and Obsidium, to pack their implants.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT38 installed a port monitoring tool, MAPMAKER, to print the active TCP connections on the local system.
Uses T1056 Input Capture: APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to capture keystrokes from the victim’s machine.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT38 leveraged Sysmon to understand the processes, services in the organization.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: APT38 has used a command-line tunneler, NACHOCHEESE, to give them shell access to a victim’s machine.
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal on Host: APT38 clears Window Event logs and Sysmon logs from the system.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: APT38 used a backdoor, QUICKRIDE, to communicate to the C2 server over HTTP and HTTPS.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: APT38 used a backdoor, NESTEGG, that has the capability to download and upload files to and from a victim’s machine.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: APT38 has used a utility called CLOSESHAVE that can securely delete a file from the system.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: APT38 uses a tool called CLEANTOAD that has the capability to modify Registry keys.
Uses T1115 Clipboard Data: APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to collect data from the clipboard.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: APT38 has conducted watering holes schemes to gain initial access to victims.
Uses T1485 Data Destruction: APT38 has used a custom secure delete function to make deleted files unrecoverable.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: APT38 has used Hermes ransomware to encrypt files with AES256.
Uses T1487 Disk Structure Wipe: APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK to render systems inoperable.
Uses T1492 Stored Data Manipulation: APT38 has used DYEPACK to create, delete, and alter records in databases used for SWIFT transactions.
Uses T1493 Transmitted Data Manipulation: APT38 has used DYEPACK to manipulate SWIFT messages en route to a printer.
Uses T1494 Runtime Data Manipulation: APT38 has used DYEPACK.FOX to manipulate PDF data as it is accessed to remove traces of fraudulent SWIFT transactions from the data displayed to the end user.
Uses T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK, which will initiate a system reboot after wiping the victim's MBR.

title: ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
text:
ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
Associated names: Chafer.
APT39 is an Iranian cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2014. They have targeted the telecommunication and travel industries to collect personal information that aligns with Iran's national priorities.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: APT39 has used WinRAR and 7-Zip to compress an archive stolen data.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: APT39 has used Mimikatz, Ncrack, Windows Credential Editor and ProcDump to dump credentials.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: APT39 has used nbtscan to discover vulnerable systems.
Uses T1021 Remote Services: APT39 used secure shell (SSH) to move laterally among their targets.
Uses T1023 Shortcut Modification: APT39 has modified LNK shortcuts.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT39 used Remexi to collect usernames from the system.
Uses T1045 Software Packing: APT39 has repacked a modified version of Mimikatz to thwart anti-virus detection.
Uses T1046 Network Service Scanning: APT39 used a custom port scanner known as BLUETORCH
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: APT39 has created scheduled tasks.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT39 has maintained persistence using the startup folder.
Uses T1064 Scripting: APT39 utilized custom scripts to perform internal reconnaissance.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT39 has been seen using RDP for lateral movement and persistence.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT39 has used stolen credentials to compromise Outlook Web Access (OWA).
Uses T1090 Connection Proxy: APT39 used custom tools to create SOCK5 proxies between infected hosts.
Uses T1100 Web Shell: APT39 has installed ANTAK and ASPXSPY web shells.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: APT39 leveraged spearphishing emails with malicious links to initially compromise victims.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: APT39 leveraged spearphishing emails with malicious attachments to initially compromise victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
text:
ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
Uses T1204 User Execution: APT39 has sent spearphishing emails in an attempt to lure users to click on a malicious attachment or link.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
APT41 is a group that carries out Chinese state-sponsored espionage activity in addition to financially motivated activity. APT41 has been active since as early as 2012. The group has been observed targeting healthcare, telecom, technology, and video game industries in 14 countries.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: APT41 created a RAR archive of targeted files for exfiltration.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: APT41 used the Windows Credential Editor to dump password hashes from memory and authenticate other user accounts.
Uses T1008 Fallback Channels: APT41 used the Steam community page as a fallback mechanism for C2.
Uses T1014 Rootkit: APT41 deployed rootkits on Linux systems.
Uses T1015 Accessibility Features: APT41 leveraged sticky keys to establish persistence.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: APT41 collected MAC addresses from victim machines.
Uses T1031 Modify Existing Service: APT41 modified legitimate Windows services to install malware backdoors.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT41 used the WMIEXEC utility to execute whoami commands on remote machines.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: APT41 attempted to masquerade their files as popular anti-virus software.
Uses T1046 Network Service Scanning: APT41 used a malware variant called WIDETONE to conduct port scans on the specified subnets.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: APT41 used WMI in several ways, including for execution of commands via WMIEXEC as well as for persistence via PowerSploit.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT41 used the netstat command as part of network reconnaissance. The group has also used a malware variant, HIGHNOON, to enumerate active RDP sessions.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: APT41 used a compromised account to create a scheduled task on a system.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT41 malware TIDYELF loaded the main WINTERLOVE component by injecting it into the iexplore.exe process.
Uses T1056 Input Capture: APT41 used a keylogger called GEARSHIFT on a target system.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: APT41 used cmd.exe /c to execute commands on remote machines.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT41 created and modified startup files for persistence.
Uses T1067 Bootkit: APT41 deployed Master Boot Record bootkits on Windows systems to hide their malware and maintain persistence on victim systems.
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal on Host: APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by clearing Windows security and system events.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: APT41 used DNS for C2 communications.
Uses T1073 DLL Side-Loading: APT41 used legitimate executables to perform DLL side-loading of their malware.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT41 used RDP for lateral movement.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT41 used compromised credentials to log on to other systems.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: APT41 leveraged PowerShell to deploy malware families in victims’ environments.
Uses T1090 Connection Proxy: APT41 used a tool called CLASSFON to covertly proxy network communications.
Uses T1102 Web Service: APT41 used legitimate websites for C2 through dead drop resolvers (DDR), including GitHub, Pastebin, and Microsoft TechNet.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: APT41 deleted files from the system.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: APT41 performed password brute-force attacks on the local admin account.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: APT41 used a malware variant called GOODLUCK to modify the registry in order to steal credentials.
Uses T1116 Code Signing: APT41 leveraged code-signing certificates to sign malware when targeting both gaming and non-gaming organizations.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: APT41 compromised an online billing/payment service using VPN access between a third-party service provider and the targeted payment service.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: APT41 used the net share command as part of network reconnaissance.
Uses T1136 Create Account: APT41 created user accounts and adds them to the User and Admin groups.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1146 Clear Command History: APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by deleting Bash histories.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: APT41 sent spearphishing emails with attachments such as compiled HTML (.chm) files to initially compromise their victims.
Uses T1195 Supply Chain Compromise: APT41 gained access to production environments where they could inject malicious code into legitimate, signed files and widely distribute them to end users.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT41 leveraged the follow exploits in their operations: CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2015-1641, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882, and CVE-2019-3396.
Uses T1223 Compiled HTML File: APT41 used compiled HTML (.chm) files for targeting.
Uses T1483 Domain Generation Algorithms: APT41 used DGA to change their C2 servers monthly.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: APT41 used a ransomware called Encryptor RaaS to encrypt files on the targeted systems and provide a ransom note to the user.
Uses T1496 Resource Hijacking: APT41 deployed a Monero cryptocurrency mining tool in a victim’s environment.

title: ATT&CK Group G0001: Axiom
text:
ATT&CK Group G0001: Axiom
Associated names: Group 72.
Axiom is a cyber espionage group suspected to be associated with the Chinese government. It is responsible for the Operation SMN campaign. Though both this group and Winnti Group use the malware Winnti, the two groups appear to be distinct based on differences in reporting on the groups' TTPs and targeting.
Uses T1001 Data Obfuscation: The Axiom group has used other forms of obfuscation, include commingling legitimate traffic with communications traffic so that network streams appear legitimate. Some malware that has been used by Axiom also uses steganography to hide communication in PNG image files.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: Axiom has been known to dump credentials.
Uses T1015 Accessibility Features: Axiom actors have been known to use the Sticky Keys replacement within RDP sessions to obtain persistence.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: The Axiom group is known to have used RDP during operations.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Axiom has been observed using SQL injection to gain access to systems.

title: ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
text:
ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
Associated names: REDBALDKNIGHT, Tick.
BRONZE BUTLER is a cyber espionage group with likely Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2008. The group primarily targets Japanese organizations, particularly those in government, biotechnology, electronics manufacturing, and industrial chemistry.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: BRONZE BUTLER has compressed data into password-protected RAR archives prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: BRONZE BUTLER has used various tools to perform credential dumping.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: BRONZE BUTLER has exfiltrated files stolen from local systems.
Uses T1009 Binary Padding: BRONZE BUTLER downloader code has included "0" characters at the end of the file to inflate the file size in a likely attempt to evade anti-virus detection.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER typically use ping and Net to enumerate systems.
Uses T1022 Data Encrypted: BRONZE BUTLER has compressed and encrypted data into password-protected RAR archives prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1024 Custom Cryptographic Protocol: BRONZE BUTLER has used a tool called RarStar that encodes data with a custom XOR algorithm when posting it to a C2 server.
Uses T1032 Standard Cryptographic Protocol: BRONZE BUTLER has used RC4 encryption (for Datper malware) and AES (for xxmm malware) to obfuscate HTTP traffic.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: BRONZE BUTLER has given malware the same name as an existing file on the file share server to cause users to unwittingly launch and install the malware on additional systems.
Uses T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive: BRONZE BUTLER has exfiltrated files stolen from file shares.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: BRONZE BUTLER has used at and schtasks to register a scheduled task to execute malware during lateral movement.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: BRONZE BUTLER uses the command-line interface.

title: ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
text:
ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: BRONZE BUTLER has used a batch script that adds a Registry Run key to establish malware persistence.
Uses T1064 Scripting: BRONZE BUTLER has used VBS, VBE, and batch scripts for execution.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: BRONZE BUTLER malware has used HTTP for C2.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has collected a list of files from the victim and uploaded it to its C2 server, and then created a new list of specific files to steal.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: BRONZE BUTLER has used PowerShell for execution.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has used net user /domain to identify account information.
Uses T1088 Bypass User Account Control: BRONZE BUTLER malware xxmm contains a UAC bypass tool for privilege escalation.
Uses T1097 Pass the Ticket: BRONZE BUTLER has created forged Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) and Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets to maintain administrative access.
Uses T1102 Web Service: BRONZE BUTLER's MSGET downloader uses a dead drop resolver to access malicious payloads.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: BRONZE BUTLER has used various tools to download files, including DGet (a similar tool to wget).
Uses T1107 File Deletion: The BRONZE BUTLER uploader or malware the uploader uses command to delete the RAR archives after they have been exfiltrated.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: BRONZE BUTLER has used a tool to capture screenshots.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has used net time to check the local time on a target system.
Uses T1132 Data Encoding: Several BRONZE BUTLER tools encode data with base64 when posting it to a C2 server.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: BRONZE BUTLER downloads encoded payloads and decodes them on the victim.

title: ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
text:
ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: BRONZE BUTLER compromised three Japanese websites using a Flash exploit to perform watering hole attacks.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: BRONZE BUTLER used spearphishing emails with malicious Microsoft Word attachments to infect victims.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: BRONZE BUTLER has exploited Microsoft Word vulnerability CVE-2014-4114 for execution.
Uses T1204 User Execution: BRONZE BUTLER has attempted to get users to launch malicious Microsoft Word attachments delivered via spearphishing emails.

title: ATT&CK Group G0063: BlackOasis
text:
ATT&CK Group G0063: BlackOasis
BlackOasis is a Middle Eastern threat group that is believed to be a customer of Gamma Group. The group has shown interest in prominent figures in the United Nations, as well as opposition bloggers, activists, regional news correspondents, and think tanks. A group known by Microsoft as NEODYMIUM is reportedly associated closely with BlackOasis operations, but evidence that the group names are aliases has not been identified.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: BlackOasis's first stage shellcode contains a NOP sled with alternative instructions that was likely designed to bypass antivirus tools.

title: ATT&CK Group G0008: Carbanak
text:
ATT&CK Group G0008: Carbanak
Associated names: Anunak, Carbon Spider.
Carbanak is a threat group that mainly targets banks. It also refers to malware of the same name (Carbanak). It is sometimes referred to as FIN7, but these appear to be two groups using the same Carbanak malware and are therefore tracked separately.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: Carbanak malware names itself "svchost.exe," which is the name of the Windows shared service host program.
Uses T1050 New Service: Carbanak malware installs itself as a service to provide persistence and SYSTEM privileges.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Carbanak actors used legitimate credentials of banking employees to perform operations that sent them millions of dollars.
Uses T1085 Rundll32: Carbanak installs VNC server software that executes through rundll32.
Uses T1089 Disabling Security Tools: Carbanak may use netsh to add local firewall rule exceptions.
Uses T1102 Web Service: Carbanak has used a VBScript named "ggldr" that uses Google Apps Script, Sheets, and Forms services for C2.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: Carbanak used legitimate programs such as AmmyAdmin and Team Viewer for remote interactive C2 to target systems.

title: ATT&CK Group G0058: Charming Kitten
text:
ATT&CK Group G0058: Charming Kitten
Charming Kitten is an Iranian cyber espionage group that has been active since approximately 2014. They appear to focus on targeting individuals of interest to Iran who work in academic research, human rights, and media, with most victims having been located in Iran, the US, Israel, and the UK. Charming Kitten usually tries to access private email and Facebook accounts, and sometimes establishes a foothold on victim computers as a secondary objective. The group's TTPs overlap extensively with another group, Magic Hound, resulting in reporting that may not distinguish between the two groups' activities.

title: ATT&CK Group G0003: Cleaver
text:
ATT&CK Group G0003: Cleaver
Associated names: Threat Group 2889, TG-2889.
Cleaver is a threat group that has been attributed to Iranian actors and is responsible for activity tracked as Operation Cleaver. Strong circumstantial evidence suggests Cleaver is linked to Threat Group 2889 (TG-2889).
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: Cleaver has been known to dump credentials.

title: ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
Associated names: Cobalt Gang, Cobalt Spider.
Cobalt Group is a financially motivated threat group that has primarily targeted financial institutions. The group has conducted intrusions to steal money via targeting ATM systems, card processing, payment systems and SWIFT systems. Cobalt Group has mainly targeted banks in Eastern Europe, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia. One of the alleged leaders was arrested in Spain in early 2018, but the group still appears to be active. The group has been known to target organizations in order to use their access to then compromise additional victims. Reporting indicates there may be links between Cobalt Group and both the malware Carbanak and the group Carbanak.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Cobalt Group obfuscated several scriptlets and code used on the victim’s machine, including through use of XOR and RC4.
Uses T1032 Standard Cryptographic Protocol: Cobalt Group has used the Plink utility to create SSH tunnels.
Uses T1037 Logon Scripts: Cobalt Group has added persistence by registering the file name for the next stage malware under UserInitMprLogonScript.
Uses T1046 Network Service Scanning: Cobalt Group leveraged an open-source tool called SoftPerfect Network Scanner to perform network scanning.
Uses T1050 New Service: Cobalt Group has created new services to establish persistence.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: Cobalt Group has created Windows tasks to establish persistence.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: Cobalt Group has injected code into trusted processes.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: Cobalt Group has used a JavaScript backdoor that is capable of launching cmd.exe to execute shell commands.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Cobalt Group has used Registry Run keys for persistence. The group has also set a Startup path to launch the PowerShell shell command and download Cobalt Strike.

title: ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
Uses T1063 Security Software Discovery: Cobalt Group used a JavaScript backdoor that is capable of collecting a list of the security solutions installed on the victim's machine.
Uses T1064 Scripting: Cobalt Group has sent Word OLE compound documents with malicious obfuscated VBA macros that will run upon user execution and executed JavaScript scriptlets on the victim's machine. The group has also used an exploit toolkit known as Threadkit that launches.bat …
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: Cobalt Group has used exploits to increase their levels of rights and privileges.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: Cobalt Group has used HTTPS and DNS tunneling for C2. The group has also used the Plink utility to create SSH tunnels.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: Cobalt Group has used Remote Desktop Protocol to conduct lateral movement.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: Cobalt Group has used powershell.exe to download and execute scripts.
Uses T1088 Bypass User Account Control: Cobalt Group has bypassed UAC.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: Cobalt Group has used public sites such as github.com and sendspace.com to upload files and then download them to victim computers. The group's JavaScript backdoor is also capable of downloading files.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: Cobalt Group deleted the DLL dropper from the victim’s machine to cover their tracks.
Uses T1108 Redundant Access: Cobalt Group has used TeamViewer to preserve remote access in case control using the Cobalt Strike module was lost.
Uses T1117 Regsvr32: Cobalt Group has used regsvr32.exe to execute scripts.
Uses T1173 Dynamic Data Exchange: Cobalt Group has sent malicious Word OLE compound documents to victims.
Uses T1191 CMSTP: Cobalt Group has used the command cmstp.exe /s /ns C:\Users\ADMINI~W\AppData\Local\Temp\XKNqbpzl.txt to bypass AppLocker and launch a malicious script.

title: ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: Cobalt Group has sent emails with URLs pointing to malicious documents.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: Cobalt Group has sent spearphishing emails with various attachment types to corporate and personal email accounts of victim organizations. Attachment types have included.rtf,.doc,.xls, archives containing LNK files, and password protected archives containing.exe and.scr executables.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Cobalt Group had exploited multiple vulnerabilities for execution, including Microsoft’s Equation Editor (CVE-2017-11882), an Internet Explorer vulnerability (CVE-2018-8174), CVE-2017-8570, CVE-2017-0199, and CVE-2017-8759.
Uses T1204 User Execution: Cobalt Group has sent emails containing malicious attachments or links that require users to execute a file or macro to infect the victim machine.
Uses T1218 Signed Binary Proxy Execution: Cobalt Group has used odbcconf to proxy the execution of malicious DLL files.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: Cobalt Group used the Ammyy Admin tool as well as TeamViewer for remote access.
Uses T1220 XSL Script Processing: Cobalt Group used msxsl.exe to bypass AppLocker and to invoke Jscript code from an XSL file.

title: ATT&CK Group G0052: CopyKittens
text:
ATT&CK Group G0052: CopyKittens
CopyKittens is an Iranian cyber espionage group that has been operating since at least 2013. It has targeted countries including Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the U.S., Jordan, and Germany. The group is responsible for the campaign known as Operation Wilted Tulip.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: CopyKittens uses ZPP, a.NET console program, to compress files with ZIP.
Uses T1022 Data Encrypted: CopyKittens encrypts data with a substitute cipher prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1085 Rundll32: CopyKittens uses rundll32 to load various tools on victims, including a lateral movement tool named Vminst, Cobalt Strike, and shellcode.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: CopyKittens has used PowerShell Empire.
Uses T1116 Code Signing: CopyKittens digitally signed an executable with a stolen certificate from legitimate company AI Squared.
Uses T1143 Hidden Window: CopyKittens has used -w hidden and -windowstyle hidden to conceal PowerShell windows.

title: ATT&CK Group G0070: Dark Caracal
text:
ATT&CK Group G0070: Dark Caracal
Dark Caracal is threat group that has been attributed to the Lebanese General Directorate of General Security (GDGS) and has operated since at least 2012.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Dark Caracal collected complete contents of the 'Pictures' folder from compromised Windows systems.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Dark Caracal has obfuscated strings in Bandook by base64 encoding, and then encrypting them.
Uses T1045 Software Packing: Dark Caracal has used UPX to pack Bandook.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Dark Caracal's version of Bandook adds a registry key to HKEY_USERS\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run for persistence.
Uses T1064 Scripting: Dark Caracal has used macros in Word documents that would download a second stage if executed.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: Dark Caracal's version of Bandook communicates with their server over a TCP port using HTTP payloads Base64 encoded and suffixed with the string “&&&”.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Dark Caracal collected file listings of all default Windows directories.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: Dark Caracal took screen shots using their Windows malware.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Dark Caracal leveraged a watering hole to serve up malicious code.
Uses T1194 Spearphishing via Service: Dark Caracal spearphished victims via Facebook and Whatsapp.
Uses T1204 User Execution: Dark Caracal makes their malware look like Flash Player, Office, or PDF documents in order to entice a user to click on it.
Uses T1223 Compiled HTML File: Dark Caracal leveraged a compiled HTML file that contained a command to download and run an executable.

title: ATT&CK Group G0079: DarkHydrus
text:
ATT&CK Group G0079: DarkHydrus
DarkHydrus is a threat group that has targeted government agencies and educational institutions in the Middle East since at least 2016. The group heavily leverages open-source tools and custom payloads for carrying out attacks.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: DarkHydrus leveraged PowerShell to download and execute additional scripts for execution.
Uses T1143 Hidden Window: DarkHydrus has used -WindowStyle Hidden to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1187 Forced Authentication: DarkHydrus used Template Injection to launch an authentication window for users to enter their credentials.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: DarkHydrus has sent spearphishing emails with password-protected RAR archives containing malicious Excel Web Query files (.iqy). The group has also sent spearphishing emails that contained malicious Microsoft Office documents that use the “attachedTemplate” technique to load a template from a …
Uses T1204 User Execution: DarkHydrus has sent malware that required users to hit the enable button in Microsoft Excel to allow an.iqy file to be downloaded.
Uses T1221 Template Injection: DarkHydrus used an open-source tool, Phishery, to inject malicious remote template URLs into Microsoft Word documents and then sent them to victims to enable Forced Authentication.

title: ATT&CK Group G0012: Darkhotel
text:
ATT&CK Group G0012: Darkhotel
Darkhotel is a threat group that has been active since at least 2004. The group has conducted activity on hotel and business center Wi‑Fi and physical connections as well as peer-to-peer and file sharing networks. The actors have also conducted spearphishing.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Darkhotel has collected the IP address and network adapter information from the victim’s machine.
Uses T1023 Shortcut Modification: Darkhotel has dropped an mspaint.lnk shortcut to disk which launches a shell script that downloads and executes a file.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Darkhotel has obfuscated code used in an operation using RC4 and other methods.
Uses T1056 Input Capture: Darkhotel has used a keylogger.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Darkhotel has searched for anti-malware strings and anti-virus processes running on the system.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Darkhotel has been known to establish persistence by adding programs to the Run Registry key.
Uses T1063 Security Software Discovery: Darkhotel has searched for anti-malware strings and anti-virus processes running on the system.
Uses T1064 Scripting: Darkhotel has dropped an mspaint.lnk shortcut to disk which launches a shell script that downloads and executes a file.
Uses T1080 Taint Shared Content: Darkhotel used a virus that propagates by infecting executables stored on shared drives.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Darkhotel has collected the hostname, OS version, service pack version, and the processor architecture from the victim’s machine.
Uses T1091 Replication Through Removable Media: Darkhotel's selective infector modifies executables stored on removable media as a method of spreading across computers.
Uses T1116 Code Signing: Darkhotel has used code-signing certificates on its malware that are either forged due to weak keys or stolen. Darkhotel has also stolen certificates and signed backdoors and downloaders with them.

title: ATT&CK Group G0012: Darkhotel
text:
ATT&CK Group G0012: Darkhotel
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: Darkhotel has decrypted strings and imports using RC4 during execution.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Darkhotel used embedded iframes on hotel login portals to redirect selected victims to download malware.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: Darkhotel has sent spearphishing emails with malicious RAR attachments.
Uses T1204 User Execution: Darkhotel sent spearphishing emails with malicious attachments that required users to click on an image in the document to drop the malware to disk.

title: ATT&CK Group G0009: Deep Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0009: Deep Panda
Associated names: Shell Crew, WebMasters, KungFu Kittens, PinkPanther, Black Vine.
Deep Panda is a suspected Chinese threat group known to target many industries, including government, defense, financial, and telecommunications. The intrusion into healthcare company Anthem has been attributed to Deep Panda. This group is also known as Shell Crew, WebMasters, KungFu Kittens, and PinkPanther. Deep Panda also appears to be known as Black Vine based on the attribution of both group names to the Anthem intrusion. Some analysts track Deep Panda and APT19 as the same group, but it is unclear from open source information if the groups are the same.
Uses T1015 Accessibility Features: Deep Panda has used the sticky-keys technique to bypass the RDP login screen on remote systems during intrusions.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Deep Panda has used ping to identify other machines of interest.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: The Deep Panda group is known to utilize WMI for lateral movement.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Deep Panda uses the Microsoft Tasklist utility to list processes running on systems.
Uses T1064 Scripting: Deep Panda has used PowerShell scripts to download and execute programs in memory, without writing to disk.
Uses T1066 Indicator Removal from Tools: Deep Panda has updated and modified its malware, resulting in different hash values that evade detection.
Uses T1077 Windows Admin Shares: Deep Panda uses net.exe to connect to network shares using net use commands with compromised credentials.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: Deep Panda has used PowerShell scripts to download and execute programs in memory, without writing to disk.
Uses T1100 Web Shell: Deep Panda uses Web shells on publicly accessible Web servers to access victim networks.
Uses T1117 Regsvr32: Deep Panda has used regsvr32.exe to execute a server variant of Derusbi in victim networks.

title: ATT&CK Group G0009: Deep Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0009: Deep Panda
Uses T1143 Hidden Window: Deep Panda has used -w hidden to conceal PowerShell windows by setting the WindowStyle parameter to hidden.

title: ATT&CK Group G0017: DragonOK
text:
ATT&CK Group G0017: DragonOK
DragonOK is a threat group that has targeted Japanese organizations with phishing emails. Due to overlapping TTPs, including similar custom tools, DragonOK is thought to have a direct or indirect relationship with the threat group Moafee. It is known to use a variety of malware, including Sysget/HelloBridge, PlugX, PoisonIvy, FormerFirstRat, NFlog, and NewCT.

title: ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
Associated names: Energetic Bear.
Dragonfly is a cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2011. They initially targeted defense and aviation companies but shifted to focus on the energy sector in early 2013. They have also targeted companies related to industrial control systems. 

A similar group emerged in 2015 and was identified by Symantec as Dragonfly 2.0. There is debate over the extent of the overlap between Dragonfly and Dragonfly 2.0, but there is sufficient evidence to lead to these being tracked as two separate groups.

title: ATT&CK Group G0074: Dragonfly 2.0
text:
ATT&CK Group G0074: Dragonfly 2.0
Associated names: Berserk Bear.
Dragonfly 2.0 is a suspected Russian group that has targeted government entities and multiple U.S. critical infrastructure sectors since at least March 2016. There is debate over the extent of overlap between Dragonfly 2.0 and Dragonfly, but there is sufficient evidence to lead to these being tracked as two separate groups.
Uses T1002 Data Compressed: Dragonfly 2.0 compressed data into.zip files prior to exfiltrating it.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: Dragonfly 2.0 dropped and executed SecretsDump and CrackMapExec, tools that can dump password hashes.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Dragonfly 2.0 collected data from local victim systems.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Dragonfly 2.0 queried the Registry to identify victim information.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 used batch scripts to enumerate network information, including information about trusts, zones, and the domain.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 likely obtained a list of hosts in the victim environment.
Uses T1023 Shortcut Modification: Dragonfly 2.0 manipulated.lnk files to gather user credentials in conjunction with Forced Authentication.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 used the command query user on victim hosts.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: Dragonfly 2.0 created accounts disguised as legitimate backup and service accounts as well as an email administration account.
Uses T1043 Commonly Used Port: Dragonfly 2.0 used SMB over ports 445 or 139 for C2. The group also established encrypted connections over port 443.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: Dragonfly 2.0 used scheduled tasks to automatically log out of created accounts every 8 hours as well as to execute malicious files.
Uses T1059 Command-Line Interface: Dragonfly 2.0 used command line for execution.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Dragonfly 2.0 added the registry value ntdll to the Registry Run key to establish persistence.

title: ATT&CK Group G0074: Dragonfly 2.0
text:
ATT&CK Group G0074: Dragonfly 2.0
Uses T1064 Scripting: Dragonfly 2.0 used various types of scripting to perform operations, including Python and batch scripts. The group was observed installing Python 2.7 on a victim.
Uses T1069 Permission Groups Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 used batch scripts to enumerate administrators in the environment.
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal on Host: Dragonfly 2.0 cleared Windows event logs and other logs produced by tools they used, including system, security, terminal services, remote services, and audit logs. The actors also deleted specific Registry keys.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: Dragonfly 2.0 used SMB for C2.
Uses T1074 Data Staged: Dragonfly 2.0 created a directory named "out" in the user's %AppData% folder and copied files to it.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: Dragonfly 2.0 moved laterally via RDP.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Dragonfly 2.0 compromised user credentials and used valid accounts for operations.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 used a batch script to gather folder and file names from victim hosts.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: Dragonfly 2.0 used PowerShell scripts for execution.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 used batch scripts to enumerate users in the victim environment.
Uses T1089 Disabling Security Tools: Dragonfly 2.0 has disabled host-based firewalls. The group has also globally opened port 3389.
Uses T1098 Account Manipulation: Dragonfly 2.0 added newly created accounts to the administrators group to maintain elevated access.
Uses T1100 Web Shell: Dragonfly 2.0 commonly created Web shells on victims' publicly accessible email and web servers, which they used to maintain access to a victim network and download additional malicious files.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: Dragonfly 2.0 copied and installed tools for operations once in the victim environment.

title: ATT&CK Group G0074: Dragonfly 2.0
text:
ATT&CK Group G0074: Dragonfly 2.0
Uses T1107 File Deletion: Dragonfly 2.0 deleted many of its files used during operations as part of cleanup, including removing applications and deleting screenshots.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: Dragonfly 2.0 dropped and executed tools used for password cracking, including Hydra.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: Dragonfly 2.0 modified the Registry to perform multiple techniques through the use of Reg.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: Dragonfly 2.0 has performed screen captures of victims, including by using a tool, scr.exe (which matched the hash of ScreenUtil).
Uses T1114 Email Collection: Dragonfly 2.0 accessed email accounts using Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: Dragonfly 2.0 used VPNs and Outlook Web Access (OWA) to maintain access to victim networks.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: Dragonfly 2.0 identified and browsed file servers in the victim network, sometimes, viewing files pertaining to ICS or Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems.
Uses T1136 Create Account: Dragonfly 2.0 created accounts on victims, including administrator accounts, some of which appeared to be tailored to each individual staging target.
Uses T1187 Forced Authentication: Dragonfly 2.0 has gathered hashed user credentials over SMB using spearphishing attachments with external resource links and by modifying.LNK file icon resources to collect credentials from virtualized systems.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Dragonfly 2.0 compromised legitimate organizations' websites to create watering holes to compromise victims.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: Dragonfly 2.0 used spearphishing with PDF attachments containing malicious links that redirected to credential harvesting websites.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: Dragonfly 2.0 used spearphishing with Microsoft Office attachments to target victims.
Uses T1204 User Execution: Dragonfly 2.0 has used various forms of spearphishing in attempts to get users to open links or attachments.
Uses T1221 Template Injection: Dragonfly 2.0 has injected SMB URLs into malicious Word spearphishing attachments to initiate Forced Authentication.

title: ATT&CK Group G0031: Dust Storm
text:
ATT&CK Group G0031: Dust Storm
Dust Storm is a threat group that has targeted multiple industries in Japan, South Korea, the United States, Europe, and several Southeast Asian countries.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Dust Storm has used Android backdoors capable of exfiltrating specific files directly from the infected devices.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Dust Storm has encoded payloads with a single-byte XOR, both skipping the key itself and zeroing in an attempt to avoid exposing the key.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Dust Storm has used Android backdoors capable of enumerating specific files on the infected devices.

title: ATT&CK Group G0066: Elderwood
text:
ATT&CK Group G0066: Elderwood
Associated names: Elderwood Gang, Beijing Group, Sneaky Panda.
Elderwood is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group that was reportedly responsible for the 2009 Google intrusion known as Operation Aurora. The group has targeted defense organizations, supply chain manufacturers, human rights and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and IT service providers.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Elderwood has encrypted documents and malicious executables.
Uses T1045 Software Packing: Elderwood has packed malware payloads before delivery to victims.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: The Ritsol backdoor trojan used by Elderwood can download files onto a compromised host from a remote location.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Elderwood has delivered zero-day exploits and malware to victims by injecting malicious code into specific public Web pages visited by targets within a particular sector.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: Elderwood has delivered zero-day exploits and malware to victims via targeted emails containing a link to malicious content hosted on an uncommon Web server.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: Elderwood has delivered zero-day exploits and malware to victims via targeted emails containing malicious attachments.
Uses T1195 Supply Chain Compromise: Elderwood has targeted manufacturers in the supply chain for the defense industry.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Elderwood has used exploitation of endpoint software, including Microsoft Internet Explorer Adobe Flash vulnerabilities, to gain execution. They have also used zero-day exploits.
Uses T1204 User Execution: Elderwood has leveraged multiple types of spearphishing in order to attempt to get a user to open links and attachments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0020: Equation
text:
ATT&CK Group G0020: Equation
Equation is a sophisticated threat group that employs multiple remote access tools. The group is known to use zero-day exploits and has developed the capability to overwrite the firmware of hard disk drives.
Uses T1109 Component Firmware: Equation is known to have the capability to overwrite the firmware on hard drives from some manufacturers.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: Equation has used tools with the functionality to search for specific information about the attached hard drive that could be used to identify and overwrite the firmware.
Uses T1480 Execution Guardrails: Equation has been observed utilizing environmental keying in payload delivery.

title: ATT&CK Group G0051: FIN10
text:
ATT&CK Group G0051: FIN10
FIN10 is a financially motivated threat group that has targeted organizations in North America since at least 2013 through 2016. The group uses stolen data exfiltrated from victims to extort organizations.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: FIN10 has used Meterpreter to enumerate users on remote systems.
Uses T1053 Scheduled Task: FIN10 has established persistence by using S4U tasks as well as the Scheduled Task option in PowerShell Empire.
Uses T1060 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: FIN10 has established persistence by using the Registry option in PowerShell Empire to add a Run key.
Uses T1064 Scripting: FIN10 has executed malicious.bat files containing PowerShell commands.
Uses T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol: FIN10 has used RDP to move laterally to systems in the victim environment.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: FIN10 has used stolen credentials to connect remotely to victim networks using VPNs protected with only a single factor. The group has also moved laterally using the Local Administrator account.
Uses T1086 PowerShell: FIN10 uses PowerShell for execution as well as PowerShell Empire to establish persistence.
Uses T1105 Remote File Copy: FIN10 has deployed Meterpreter stagers and SplinterRAT instances in the victim network after moving laterally.
Uses T1107 File Deletion: FIN10 has used batch scripts and scheduled tasks to delete critical system files.

title: ATT&CK Group G0085: FIN4
text:
ATT&CK Group G0085: FIN4
FIN4 is a financially-motivated threat group that has targeted confidential information related to the public financial market, particularly regarding healthcare and pharmaceutical companies, since at least 2013. FIN4 is unique in that they do not infect victims with typical persistent malware, but rather they focus on capturing credentials authorized to access email and other non-public correspondence.
Uses T1056 Input Capture: FIN4 has captured credentials via fake Outlook Web App (OWA) login pages and has also used a.NET based keylogger.
Uses T1064 Scripting: FIN4 has used VBA macros to display a dialog box and collect victim credentials.
Uses T1071 Standard Application Layer Protocol: FIN4 has used HTTP POST requests to transmit data.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: FIN4 has used legitimate credentials to hijack email communications.
Uses T1114 Email Collection: FIN4 has accessed and hijacked email communications using stolen credentials.
Uses T1141 Input Prompt: FIN4 has presented victims with spoofed Windows Authentication prompts to collect their credentials.
Uses T1188 Multi-hop Proxy: FIN4 has used Tor to log in to victims' email accounts.
Uses T1192 Spearphishing Link: FIN4 has used spearphishing emails (often sent from compromised accounts) containing malicious links.
Uses T1193 Spearphishing Attachment: FIN4 has used spearphishing emails containing attachments (which are often stolen, legitimate documents sent from compromised accounts) with embedded malicious macros.
Uses T1204 User Execution: FIN4 has lured victims to launch malicious attachments and click malicious links delivered via spearphishing emails (often sent from compromised accounts).
Uses T1492 Stored Data Manipulation: FIN4 has created rules in victims' Microsoft Outlook accounts to automatically delete emails containing words such as “hacked," "phish," and “malware" in a likely attempt to prevent organizations from communicating about their activities.

title: ATT&CK Group G0053: FIN5
text:
ATT&CK Group G0053: FIN5
FIN5 is a financially motivated threat group that has targeted personally identifiable information and payment card information. The group has been active since at least 2008 and has targeted the restaurant, gaming, and hotel industries. The group is made up of actors who likely speak Russian.
Uses T1003 Credential Dumping: FIN5 has dumped credentials from victims. Specifically, the group has used the tool GET5 Penetrator to look for remote login and hard-coded credentials.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: FIN5 has used the open source tool Essential NetTools to map the network and build a list of targets.
Uses T1064 Scripting: FIN5 scans processes on all victim systems in the environment and uses automated scripts to pull back the results.
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal on Host: FIN5 has cleared event logs from victims.
Uses T1074 Data Staged: FIN5 scripts save memory dump data into a specific directory on hosts in the victim environment.
